questions.q: In tag-based masking, which statement actually attaches a masking policy so that protection goes live?
options: CREATE TAG ... ALLOWED_VALUES
GRANT MASKING POLICY TO TAG
ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... SET TAG
ALTER TAG ... SET MASKING POLICY
questions.explain: ALTER TAG ... SET MASKING POLICY binds a masking policy to the tag itself — the step that actually turns masking on for every tagged column.

questions.q: Why does tags.tasty_pii in this lesson need two separate masking policies attached to it?
options: Snowflake requires exactly two policies on every tag, no matter what
One policy is for production and one is for development
A tag can hold at most one masking policy per data type, and the tagged columns span two types (string and date)
Masking policies always come in pairs
questions.explain: A tag may carry at most one masking policy per data type. Since tasty_pii tags both VARCHAR columns and a DATE column, it needs one STRING policy and one DATE policy.

questions.q: What happens to a brand-new column that is tagged with tags.tasty_pii six months after the masking policy was attached to the tag?
options: Masking only applies to columns tagged before the policy was attached
It is protected automatically — no new ALTER TABLE ... SET MASKING POLICY statement is needed
The tag assignment fails because the tag already has a policy
It stays unmasked until someone manually reattaches the policy to that column
questions.explain: That's the core advantage of tag-based masking: any column tagged with a tag that already has a masking policy attached is protected immediately and automatically.

questions.q: What does a tag's ALLOWED_VALUES list control?
options: The set of values a column may be tagged with — an unlisted value is rejected
How many columns a single tag may be applied to
Which roles are allowed to query the tagged column
Which masking policy applies to which row
questions.explain: ALLOWED_VALUES constrains what a tag can be set to when applied, keeping tagging consistent instead of drifting into free-text values.

questions.q: Compared to the column-by-column masking approach from Lesson 7, what is the main advantage of tag-based masking shown in this lesson?
options: Tag-based masking does not require a masking policy to be created first
Tag-based masking only works on downstream views, not base tables
One ALTER TAG statement protects every column carrying the tag, instead of repeating ALTER TABLE per column
Tag-based masking is faster to query at runtime
questions.explain: The lesson's central contrast: Lesson 7's approach requires a separate ALTER TABLE statement per column, while tag-based masking requires only one ALTER TAG statement to cover every tagged column, present and future.
